lede: My Master's research: can duplicate questions be detected accurately without the heavy models? FastText embeddings plus PCA kept 83.68% accuracy while cutting training time by two thirds and memory by 83%.

facts.label: Context
facts.value: Master of Science in AI, UMPSA (Master Project II)

sections.headline: Accurate enough, and cheap enough to run.

body: Duplicate questions fragment answers and waste moderators' time on large Q&A platforms. The strongest published detectors use deep models like BERT and BiLSTMs, which are accurate but expensive to train and serve.
This research asked a narrower, practical question: how much accuracy do you actually lose if you compress the features aggressively, and what do you gain in speed and memory?

sections.headline: High-dimensional vectors are slow at scale.

items.title: Manual detection does not scale
items.detail: Semantically identical questions are phrased differently, so keyword matching misses them.

items.title: Heavy features, heavy costs
items.detail: Pair features built from word embeddings reach 1,200 dimensions, which slows training and inference.

items.title: A gap in the literature
items.detail: Most prior work reports accuracy and ignores computational efficiency entirely.

sections.headline: Compress the meaning, keep the signal.

body: Represent each question with FastText word vectors, combine the pair into features, then use Principal Component Analysis to shrink those features before classification, and measure both accuracy and cost.

sections.headline: From raw text to a duplicate score.

value.label: Duplicate detection pipeline
value.caption: Evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall and F1, plus training time, memory and inference speed.

nodes.title: Preprocess
nodes.detail: Cleaning, tokenisation, lemmatisation; question words like how and why kept.

nodes.title: Pair features
nodes.detail: Absolute differences and element-wise products: 1,200 features.

nodes.title: Classifier
nodes.detail: Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost.

body: FastText separated the classes clearly: duplicate pairs averaged a similarity of 0.742 against 0.431 for non-duplicates. PCA at 200 dimensions kept 89.5% of the variance while shrinking the features by 83.3%.

value.caption: Computational efficiency · 200D vs full 1,200D features
value.note: Memory for feature storage fell from 3.2 GB to 0.53 GB (83.4%) for every model.

items.title: Four dimension settings
items.detail: 50, 100, 150 and 200 dimensions, each tested against the full baseline.

items.title: Four classifiers
items.detail: Linear and ensemble models compared on the same features.

items.title: Question-aware cleaning
items.detail: Interrogative words were kept because they carry intent.

items.title: Cost as a metric
items.detail: Training time, memory and inference speed measured alongside accuracy.

body: Deep-learning approaches in the literature reach 91 to 96% accuracy, but at far higher computational cost. This framework trades a few points of accuracy for a system that is fast and light enough to run widely.

sections.headline: Measure the cost, not just the score.

items.title: The trade-off curve is the result
items.detail: Showing accuracy against dimensions said more than any single best number.

items.title: Most meaning survives compression
items.detail: Losing five sixths of the features cost a third of a percentage point.

items.title: Efficiency belongs in the evaluation
items.detail: A model that is too expensive to deploy has not really solved the problem.
